analysis.one_liner: Adds dental care, dentures, and oral health services to Medicare coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: referred to two House committees in July 2021, it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made Medicare cover dental care for the first time: routine exams, cleanings, x-rays and fluoride treatments, plus fillings, root canals, crowns, bridges and dentures, starting in 2025. Today most Medicare beneficiaries pay for dental work out of pocket or buy separate private dental insurance, because Medicare excludes routine dental care. The bill was introduced by Rep. Robin Kelly with seven Democratic cosponsors and never moved past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries, most of whom currently pay out of pocket for dental care or go without it. The bill covers preventive services like two oral exams and two cleanings per year, and phases in coverage of basic treatments (fillings, extractions) at an 80% federal payment and major treatments (crowns, root canals, dentures), with dentures covered once every five years. The benefit would be financed by a government contribution rather than by raising Part B premiums, so beneficiaries would not bear the premium cost directly.

how_it_helps.text: Adds dental and oral health services to Medicare Part B, including preventive and screening services (oral exams, cleanings, x-rays, fluoride treatments) and basic and major treatments defined by the Secretary of Health and Human Services.
Covers dentures as durable medical equipment, payable once every five years per beneficiary (more often if dentures no longer fit), starting January 1, 2025.
Sets the federal payment at 80% for preventive services and basic treatments, and phases in major treatments from a 10% federal share in 2025 to 50% in 2029.

Finances the new benefit through a government contribution to the Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, excluding the new dental costs from the usual Part B premium calculation, so the benefit would not be charged to beneficiaries through higher premiums.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The bill specifies no dedicated tax or offset: dental benefit costs would be covered by a general-revenue government contribution, and implementation would draw $20 million a year from the Medicare trust fund for administration in fiscal years 2022 through 2027. Dentists and dental insurers would also face a changed market, with a public payer setting rates benchmarked to Medicaid, TRICARE, and Medicare Advantage payment levels.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no dedicated funding source: the new benefit would be paid for by a government contribution on top of existing Medicare financing, increasing federal deficits rather than being offset by new revenue or cuts elsewhere.

Coverage of major care starts small and ramps up slowly: in 2025 Medicare would pay only 10% of the cost of crowns, root canals, bridges and other major treatments, reaching 50% only in 2029, leaving seniors with substantial out-of-pocket costs for the most expensive care during the first four years.

Payment rates to dentists would be set by referencing what Medicaid, TRICARE, Medicare Advantage and other payers pay for comparable services, which are generally lower than private dental insurance rates; a supporter would acknowledge this could limit how many dentists accept Medicare patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to seniors is real and substantial: untreated dental disease causes pain, infection, and worse health, and dental care is one of the largest uncovered categories of medical need for older Americans. The costs are also real: this is an expensive entitlement with no offsetting revenue in the bill, and the four-year phase-in means the people most likely to need major dental work immediately would still pay most of that bill at first. A stronger version would have paired the benefit with financing and a faster phase-in.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and their Health Subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and no committee or subcommittee ever acted on it before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Robin Kelly introduced the Medicare Dental Coverage Act of 2021 on July 22, 2021, with seven Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
The bill was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and then to the Subcommittee on Health, on July 22 and 23, 2021.
That subcommittee referral was the last action of any kind on the bill; it received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the status quo remained: private dental insurers kept their market of Medicare beneficiaries buying separate dental coverage, and dental providers kept billing patients out of pocket at private rates. Taxpayers avoided the new federal spending, but seniors continued to pay for dental care out of pocket or go without it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private dental insurers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls occurred; all eight sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough to attract public opposition.

industries.note: Millions of Medicare beneficiaries buy standalone dental insurance or Medigap dental riders because Medicare excludes dental care; a universal Medicare dental benefit would replace much of that market with a public program. The insurers' revenue depends on the gap this bill would have filled, so their interest runs against the beneficiaries' interest in covered care.

The bill would create a large new stream of Medicare-covered patients, but it would exclude dentists from most Medicare performance-payment programs and set payment rates by referencing Medicaid, TRICARE, and Medicare Advantage rates, which are typically below private dental rates. More patients, but at lower reimbursement, and dentists would no longer set charges freely for Medicare patients.

Many Medicare Advantage plans advertise supplemental dental benefits as a selling point; a universal Medicare dental benefit would erase that advantage, though the bill directs the Secretary to consider Medicare Advantage payment rates when setting dentist payment, tying the new public benefit to the private plans' rates.
